Here's a focused final-round prep plan and immediate practice. One next step: tell me whether you want a timed mock now (I’ll ask the first question).
Prep highlights (what to do, in order)

2) If you have the posting or JD, paste it here so I can tailor answers and questions to what they asked for.
3) Prepare three concise stories: a team win, a hard problem you solved, and a failure or mistake with what you learned — each with a clear result (number, percent, or time saved).
4) Drill Accounting fundamentals: three quick topics below to be ready to explain clearly.
5) Drill Valuation/modeling basics: two crisp answers below you must be able to say in one or two sentences.
6) Prepare a 60-second “Tell me about yourself” that leads with a headline, then 2–3 bullets: most relevant experience/skill, one concrete result, and why Lincoln fits.
7) Prepare 2 smart questions to ask them (examples below).
8) Run a timed mock (I can run it now if you want).

Quick coaching: how to answer in this round
- Start with a 1-line headline: who you are professionally and what you bring (e.g., “I’m an analyst with X deal experience in Y sectors…”). Then 2–3 bullets: most relevant skill, one specific quantified result, and one sentence why Lincoln fits. Close with what you want in the role. Keep ~60 seconds.
Accounting to rehearse (answer aloud, brief & procedural)
- Walk me through the three financial statements and how they connect.
- If depreciation increases, what happens to the three statements in year 1? (Explain cash, income, and balance sheet impacts.)
- What is working capital and why do changes in NWC affect cash flow?

Valuation / modeling to rehearse (short crisp answers)
- Name three valuation approaches and when you use each (DCF, comparable companies, precedent transactions).
- How do you convert unlevered free cash flow to equity value? (One-sentence process: discount FCF to firm value, subtract net debt to get equity value, divide by shares for per-share.)
M&A / deal question to be ready for
- What’s accretion/dilution? Briefly explain how an acquisition can be accretive to EPS (example: buyer’s post-deal EPS rises if deal increases net income per share after accounting for deal financing and share issuance).

Behavioral story structure (use this exactly)
- One-line result first, then: Situation/task (1 sentence), Action (2–3 sentences, emphasize what you did), Result (1 sentence with a number).

Two sharp questions you can ask them
- “What does success look like for an Analyst in the first 6–12 months on your team?”
- “Which types of deals or sectors will I spend most of my time on, and how do you split modeling versus client-facing work?”
Common final-round traps
- Long unfocused stories — lead with the result.
- Over-explaining technicals without linking to deal impact — always tie back to why it mattered for the transaction.
- Not confirming next steps or timeline at the end — always ask what to expect next.

B) 6-question technical mock (I ask; you answer; I score).

replies:
You don't have any applications or a first posting on file yet. The one step that starts this is: paste the job posting link (or the job title and company exactly as listed) you want me to prepare the first application for.

If you want a sensible default so I can show the fields now, I'll assume "the first posting" is the top match from a search for the role and city you want; tell me the role and city and I'll prepare the full, field-by-field application card.

What I will submit (field-by-field) once you pick a posting — exactly what you'll see on the application card to review and approve before anything runs on your computer:
1) Job reference
- What it is: the job title and company as the posting lists them.
- Why I include it: matches the employer's record so your submission goes to the right role.
- What I need from you: no extra info unless the posting shows multiple locations or requisition numbers.

2) Location
- What it is: city / remote / on-site as the posting states.
- Why: required by many forms for routing and timezone of interview invites.
- What I do: copy exactly from the posting; ask you only if the posting allows multiple choices.
3) Your resume file
- What it is: the PDF resume chosen for this application.
- Why: main document applicants submit.
- What I need from you now: paste your resume here (or say which saved resume to use). If you paste your resume, I will read it and show the top role, skills and education I saved plus two changes to strengthen it for this posting.

4) Contact info for the resume header
- What it is: name and email shown at the top of the resume.
- Why: some forms ask to fill these separately; must match the resume.
- What I need: type the exact name and email to use (if you don't, I'll ask that one question).
5) Cover letter / pitch (optional)
- What it is: a short 1-paragraph pitch or a cover letter file if the posting requests one or there's an open text box.
- Why: tailored pitch raises match rate.
- What I do: draft a 120-word email-style pitch or a longer cover letter with [brackets] for any missing employer-specific detail; it's yours to send when you approve.
6) Answers to screening questions
- What they are: boolean or short-answer questions from the employer (e.g., authorization to work, salary range, notice period, willingness to relocate).
- Why: many forms reject on mismatched answers.
- What I do: prefill them from confirmed facts on file; for any missing answers I will show the exact question and my suggested answer and ask you to confirm. If you haven't given me these facts yet, I'll default to leaving them blank and ask you.
7) Work authorization & visa status
- What it is: citizenship or visa sponsorship requirement answers.
- Why: many roles filter automatically.
- What I need from you: your exact current authorization to work; if you don't provide it now, I'll prompt on the card.

8) Compensation expectations (if asked)
- What it is: a range or current base.
- Why: used for screening.
- What I will do: quote numbers only from posting pay if present; if not listed, I'll show the form field blank and suggest a market-appropriate range for you to approve. I will not invent pay numbers.
9) Availability / Earliest start date
- What it is: your earliest date to start.
- Why: scheduling and offers.
- What I need: tell me the date or phrase (e.g., "2 weeks"), or I'll leave blank and ask on the card.

10) Attachments (certs, portfolio, transcripts) — if requested
- What it is: any extra files the posting lists.
- What I do: list the requested attachments and show which confirmed files you have; for anything missing, I mark it as "not provided" so you can either upload or confirm skipping it.
11) Referral / source
- What it is: how you heard about the role (employee referral, job board).
- Why: some employers track source.
- What I do: default to the posting source; you can overwrite it.

12) Additional open-text answers
- What it is: employer essay or motivation fields.
- What I do: draft targeted answers using the posting text and your confirmed facts; put [brackets] where I need specifics from you (team name, measurable example, portfolio link). Each drafted answer is shown for your edit and approval.

13) Portfolio or work sample links
- What it is: URLs to relevant work.
- What I need: paste the links you want used; I will place them into the fields exactly as you give them.
14) Equal opportunity / demographic optional fields
- What it is: voluntary demographic checkboxes.
- What I do: leave these up to you; I do not fill them without explicit direction.

15) Final review & confirmation checkbox
- What it is: a line that summarizes everything that will be sent.
- What I do: show a single "Ready to queue" summary of each filled field and every unanswered required field. Nothing is submitted until you press approve in your extension.
How I handle missing information and defaults (my sensible defaults, unless you tell me otherwise):
- If you don't give a resume, I'll ask you to paste one. If you ask me to proceed anyway, I will refuse to queue until a resume is present.
- For screening questions I don't have answers for, I will leave them blank and flag them as required on the review card.
- For cover letters or essay answers I will draft suggested text with [brackets] for missing facts; you must confirm before I queue.
Next step (pick one)
- Paste the job posting link (or title + company) you want the “first one” to be, or tell me the role and city and I'll prepare the full field-by-field card now using the sensible defaults described.
